notes: The manual's wiring images are not provided (only a generic 'rpi-gpio-wiring-a-button' include and a video), so the layout is the standard one: each tactile switch straddles the breadboard centre gap, with the GPIO pin on the top-half side and ground on the bottom-half side.
Pins GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO10 come from the full code listing. The manual says any GPIO pins can be used.

The catalogue card for raspberry-pi-4 lists only a single GPIO_HEADER port. Following the task instructions, I used individual header pin names (GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO10, GND) as ports on the board. They may need to be added to the card.

Pushbutton orientation is an assumption: side 1 (1.l, 1.r) goes in the top half and side 2 (2.l, 2.r) in the bottom half. The button is wired GPIO to ground (gpiozero Button uses the internal pull-up), so no external resistor is needed.

Each of the four buttons uses its own column pair on the breadboard (3-5, 8-10, 13-15, 18-20). The bottom-half strip of each button links to the bottom negative rail (bn) with a pin-to-pin jumper. A pin-to-socket jumper joins one Pi GND pin to that rail.
For the male-to-female jumpers, the 'a' end is the female socket on the Pi pin and the 'b' end is the male pin in the breadboard.
The Pi has five pin-to-socket leads (4 GPIO + 1 GND) and four pin-to-pin leads (one ground link per button), as the manual's parts list says.

Speakers or headphones plug into the Pi's audio output. The catalogue card has no audio-jack port and the manual shows no wiring for it, so they are left out of the graph. The sounds are played in software with pygame.
